title: The Fathers on Colossians
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Paul writes against those urging Greek observances, the law, and angel worship as necessary for perfection.
comments.comment: The occasion was this. Believers who had come from among the Greeks had Greeks who were still pagans pulling them back to Greek observances. Believers from among the Jews had Jews urging them to keep the law, as though grace without the law were less than complete. The Greeks’ argument to them was that it is right to worship angels as well, for they said their gods were angels: God is great and out of human reach, and so he supplies his workings to those in need through these angels, as through go-betweens. … From all these texts Jews and Greeks alike, some of them believers and some not, drew their conclusion: the grace that comes through the Lord Jesus is superfluous, since the angels, who have been there from the beginning, are enough to bring to God those who obey; and to neglect all the observances kept by Jews and Greeks, they said, was to fall short of perfection. The apostles’ aim in the letter before us is directed against all this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the background of the letter in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul keeps naming Christ because they were setting Christ aside.
comments.comment: Notice that in a few lines he names Christ many times. Christ was the one they were setting aside, so Paul keeps mentioning him, to stamp on their souls a longing for him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul names Christ so often.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The hope of the kingdom was won by Christ, not by angels.
comments.comment: … He is already showing them that the hope laid up for us, the hope of the resurrection and of the kingdom, was not won by the administration of angels but by the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by the hope laid up in heaven.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The gospel reaching the whole world shows the power of Christ at work in the preaching.
comments.comment: … By adding “as also in all the world”, he strengthens their faith. The gospel has reached not only you, he says, but already the whole world, and that is a sign of the power of Christ at work in the preaching. “For it was not neglected; it bears fruit and grows.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by the gospel spreading and bearing fruit.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Epaphras is praised so they will listen to him.
comments.comment: He commends Epaphras as one of the saints and as the man who would instruct them, so that they would listen all the more to his teaching.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God’s will is that they know salvation comes only through Christ.
comments.comment: What was God’s will? That you should recognize and know that you cannot be saved through angels, only through Jesus Christ. How, then, are we to come to know it? In wisdom that is spiritual, not worldly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by knowing God’s will.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Endurance needs long-suffering and joy, and God rewards those who rejoice in afflictions for Christ.
comments.comment:
Above all, he joined long-suffering to endurance. Endurance does not hold firm without long-suffering, and endurance without joy earns no reward. Joy, more than anything, is needed here.

It is not the one who grieves over afflictions suffered for Christ who receives the reward from God, but the one who rejoices in them. And what is the reward? Adoption as sons, the inheritance, and a life spent with the angels.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by patience and joy in suffering.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God has brought us into the kingdom of the Son, not of angels, and Son of love means beloved Son.
comments.comment: Before the flood and after it, before the law and under the law, the angels served God for your salvation. Yet that is not how God brought us into his kingdom. It is now, through our Lord, his Only-begotten, that his kingdom has been given to us. As for “the Son of his love”: this does not mean that Christ is a son born of God’s love. Some people are called sons of disobedience (Ephesians 2:2), others sons of Gehenna (Matthew 23:15), and the devil a son of perdition; and anyone else is named the son of whatever he has run to and attached himself to. He is not a son by nature but by likeness of character. In the same way the Saviour was called Son of God’s love, because he is Son of God not by nature only but also by the true bond of love. “The Father loves the Son,” it says, “and has given all things into his hand” (John 3:35). Or it is because he loved us and suffered for us. And the phrase should be read like this: “into the kingdom of the love of his Son.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul speaks of the kingdom of the Son of love.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God the Father gave his only-begotten Son, the image of the invisible God, a share of his own greatness, since a fitting image of the invisible God must show his greatness too.
comments.comment: But in our teaching the God and Father of all is not the only one who is great. For he has given a share of himself and of his greatness to the only-begotten and “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), so that, being himself “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), he might keep the image of the Father in greatness too. For there could not have been a well-proportioned image, if I may call it that, and a beautiful image “of the invisible God,” that did not also present the image of his greatness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Christ is the image of the invisible God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Firstborn cannot be taken strictly alongside only-begotten.
comments.comment: … So “firstborn” is not used in its strict sense, since it is the opposite of “only-begotten”. By nature, the only-begotten is a father’s only child, while the firstborn has other brothers and is the first of them. The two words cannot both be taken strictly. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul uses firstborn in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ existed before all things, so hope should rest on him rather than on angels.
comments.comment: He means that Christ existed before. If he did not exist before all things, how are all things created in him? He said that all things are created in him so that we would stop putting our hope in angels and set our hope on Christ. “In him” stands for “through him”. … “All things have been created through him and for him.” This means that the cause of creation goes back to him. Or he said “for him” because nothing created is outside him; all things are held within him. “And in him all things hold together”: either “through him”, or it means that he holds all things fast by his will and power, according to the mystery hidden in God, who created all things.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul calls the Son the image of the invisible God and also firstborn from the dead, because the body he took was truly his own and so he could die in a human way for us.
comments.comment: … He [Paul] calls the Son naturally begotten from him — that is, the God Word — the image of the invisible God, and also that through him all things were brought to birth, whether visible or invisible, in heaven and on earth, and that he himself is before all things: “for in the beginning was the Word,” (John 1:1) and he is the maker of the ages, having existence older than all time. But he says that the one who is such by his own nature has been given by the Father as head of the church’s body, and that he himself is the firstborn from the dead. Then how is the God Word who always exists, in whom all things hold together, said to become firstborn from the dead and firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, unless the body taken by him is truly his own? When it has suffered death, he himself would be understood to suffer — the event having a not-implausible account in him, for what is his own has suffered. In this way he is understood as firstborn from the dead, though by nature immortal and life itself. … So when, having lowered himself into emptying, he has been given as head of the church’s body, then the one who as God does not know how to suffer death is also said to die in a human way for us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Christ has first place in all that belongs to his saving work, from obedience to rising from the dead.
comments.comment:
He called him firstborn of all creation because he existed before creation. In the same way he calls him firstborn from the dead because he rose to incorruption before the rest of the dead. No one would say that when the dead have risen they will all be Christ’s brothers, as if the title had been given with that outcome in view; most of them are sinners and ungodly. So in the earlier verse, as in this one, the sense of time is beside the point.

“That in all things he might come to have first place.” In which things? Those that belong to his saving dispensation. He was first in obedience, first in baptism, first in his way of life, first in suffering, first from the dead. So he rightly has first place in all things, since he became the beginning for those who follow him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by first place in all things.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ became firstborn from the dead by first raising his own body, and so opened a way for human nature to rise and overcome corruption.
comments.comment: … He [Christ] says that those who have believed in him have been given to him by the Father, so that he may not lose them but raise them on the last day (John 6:39). How then did he raise them, if not clearly through his own resurrection from the dead? For having made alive his own temple even before the others, and having shaken death’s power through the death of his own flesh, he became a way for human nature toward resurrection and toward being able at last to overpower corruption. So what is proper to the God-Word who came down from heaven is that through which he became firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18) — so that what was given him may also follow the raised one toward life, no longer being lost through the first-formed man’s transgression, but rather being saved through Christ’s obedience.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ is called the firstborn from the dead.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: The church as fullness dwells in Christ its head, and God reconciles all things through Christ rather than angels.
comments.comment: He calls the church “fullness”, as he has already rightly said, because it has been filled with the Holy Spirit. He says that Christ was pleased to have all the fullness dwell in him, and so through himself to reconcile all things and make them one with himself. … So God was pleased that his fullness, the church he has filled, should dwell in Christ as in its own head: that is, it should keep in step with Christ and depend on him, not on angels. For God was pleased to reconcile all things through Christ, not through angels. Indeed, everything achieved for the world was achieved through Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Plainly explains what the fullness means and how God reconciles all things through Christ rather than angels.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The one who sins is God's enemy, but God is an enemy to no one.
comments.comment: … Those sinning are his [the Savior's] enemies. This is said: 'For being enemies, we were estranged' (Colossians 1:21). The one sinning is an enemy of God, not God is an enemy of him; for God is an enemy to no one. …
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain words in what sense we were God's enemies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Son, not angels, reconciles us to God in his flesh.
comments.comment: In these words too he teaches them that it is not angels who will reconcile them to God, but the Son. For he says, “He reconciled us in the body of his flesh.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains who reconciles us to God and how.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: They should stand firm as others worldwide have done.
comments.comment: The gospel has reached not only you but the whole world, and nowhere has anyone been moved from it; they all stand firm. So you, too, must make yourselves secure now.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul’s call to continue in the faith.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul rejoices to fill up what remains of Christ’s afflictions by suffering for the church.
comments.comment: If anything is lacking as regards suffering, he says, still I am filling up what remains of the afflictions for Christ’s sake; I rejoice to suffer for you. Why “for you”? Because he suffered for preaching to them. If Christ is the head of the body, the church, then the afflictions stirred up against the church by those who rise against the word of truth are very rightly called Christ’s afflictions. So the one who distinguishes himself in these afflictions and struggles through them would not be wide of the mark to say that he is filling up, in his turn, what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by filling up Christ’s afflictions.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The mystery is Christ’s coming, and its riches free us from needing angel patronage.
comments.comment: The mystery is Christ’s saving dispensation and his becoming man. The glory of the mystery is the resurrection from the dead. The riches are the great mercy that comes from the forgiveness given in baptism, which also grants rebirth to the baptized. “What is the riches of the glory of this mystery?” Do not become poor, he says, by running to shelter under the patronage of angels. Christ, he says, has been given to us as our riches. Let us not become poor by turning to the patronage of angels.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the mystery and its riches mean for the reader.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The mystery is great and rich in glory only if Christ is God the Word, who became human and remained what he was.
comments.comment: “…Christ in you, the hope of glory, whom we proclaim.” (Colossians 1:27–28) How is the mystery hidden, or how is it God’s word at all, and what riches of glory are in it, if Christ is merely a common human as we are? The mystery is neither great nor worth naming unless we approach Christ as God and understand that the Word, being God and in the equality and form of the Father, lowered himself into emptying — becoming human and remaining what he was. Only so is the mystery thought rich and full of glory.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul calls the gospel a hidden mystery rich in glory.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The treasures are called hidden so that the unworthy do not find divine knowledge, while those who labor for it attain it.
comments.comment: … It is customary to call the things said unclearly 'hidden' because of a certain economy [a purposeful plan]; for according to this also the wisdom of God is hidden in a mystery. Just so, 'The treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden' (Colossians 2:3) have been said. And the end or purpose of these hidden things is not to let the unworthy find the knowledge of divine things, so that those having a desire for the attainment of divine knowledge, having given themselves to labors and exercises, might attain the purpose. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are called hidden.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We share in the treasures through Christ himself.
comments.comment: If the hidden treasures of knowledge are in Christ, then clearly we share in them through Christ himself, not through angels.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: We received Christ as the Word made flesh, who did not cease to be the Word and is named Lord of glory.
comments.comment: … “As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in faith.” (Colossians 2:6–7) How did we receive Christ? Wise John will teach it: “And the Word became flesh.” (John 1:14) Yet he has not ceased to be Word even though he became flesh; even so he sits with his own Father, and the crucified one is named Lord of glory. …
comments.selected_reason: Says what it means to have received Christ Jesus the Lord.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Rootedness shows firm faith, while walking means living as Christ lived.
comments.comment: “Walking” may seem to be the opposite of “being rooted”, but in this passage it is not. “Being rooted” shows all of us the unshakeable firmness of faith, while “walking in Christ” means following plainly in Christ’s footsteps by living the same life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul’s wording in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Greek philosophy holds persuasive arguments that present falsehood as truth, and Paul calls the words of the philosophers 'according to the elements of the world'.
comments.comment: Paul, then, saw that Greek philosophy holds persuasive arguments, not easy for most people to dismiss, which present falsehood as truth. Of these he says: “See to it that no one carries you off as spoil through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8). And seeing that a certain greatness shows itself in the words of the wisdom of the world (1 Corinthians 1:20), he said that the words of the philosophers were “according to the elements of the world.” …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by philosophy and the elements of the world.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The church, filled with the Godhead, dwells bodily in Christ.
comments.comment: He means the church, since it has been filled with the Godhead of the Father. The sense is this: the church is full, and it dwells in Christ bodily …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: To be filled in Christ is to be filled through Him with the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: … “And you are filled in him” stands for “filled through him”. Filled with what? Clearly, with the Holy Spirit. “Who is the head of every rule and authority”: he is head not only of the church, he says, for that belongs to his saving dispensation, but also of every invisible power, since he is its maker as well.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by filled in Him.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Fleshly circumcision is a type of the inward circumcision by the Spirit, which strips off the old self and cuts away the pleasures of the flesh.
comments.comment: For circumcision in the flesh would be a very clear type of the inward circumcision, the circumcision in the spirit (Romans 2:29), by which Christ removes all defilement from our thoughts. For, in the words of the blessed Paul, ‘we have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the flesh’ (Colossians 2:11). For when we have, as it were, stripped off the old self, which is being corrupted by deceitful desires (Ephesians 4:22), and have all but cut away the pleasures of the flesh by the keen edge and the working of the Spirit, we shall already, in some measure, show ourselves fit to be counted worthy even of seeing God, and of becoming a sacred dwelling place of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the circumcision made without hands.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Baptism is spiritual circumcision cutting away the sins of believers.
comments.comment: That is, he circumcised us from the sin of the flesh and made us alive to himself through baptism. So baptism in Christ is a spiritual circumcision, because it cuts away the sins of those who believe.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by circumcision in Christ.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: We are said to be buried and raised with Christ because the whole of human nature was in him as he trampled on death.
comments.comment: Yet the Word who is from God the Father does not give life to a temple foreign to him, nor simply to that of someone else, but rather to his own body, through which he is also said to have died for us, so that the good of the resurrection too might be found to have truly come about for us. For the whole of human nature was in him, trampling on death; this is how we are said to have been buried with him and raised with him (Colossians 2:12), and seated with him “in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how we are buried and raised with Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The baptized already share Christ’s resurrection from the death of sins.
comments.comment:
Through baptism our sins are stripped away and circumcised. “Buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him.” Those baptized in the blood of Christ confess through baptism that they share in his death, and since they have shared in his death, they will also enjoy his resurrection.

Resurrection is spoken of in two ways: one spiritual, the other bodily. All human flesh will rise because Christ rose from the dead. But those who were not baptized in Christ and died in their unbelief will share in the common resurrection without enjoying the redemption and the promise. Those who were baptized into Christ, however, have been given another resurrection even before the common one, for they have already risen from the death of their sins.
comments.selected_reason: Explains burial and raising with Christ in baptism.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Those raised from the death of sins must no longer live for the flesh.
comments.comment:
That is why he said, “in which you were also raised with him”, not “in which you will be raised with him”. Those, then, who have been raised from the death of their sins: how can they still live as people who are going to die again? Did they rise for nothing? If they live as people who will live for ever, they no longer spend their lives according to the flesh as slaves to its desires; they will live according to the Spirit.

He calls wrong deeds “the body of sin”, because they are carried out through the body. Baptism, then, is the circumcision of Christ, for it strips off the body of sin, which is the foreskin. As the foreskin is something superfluous to a Jew, so sin is to soul and body. He kept to this figure all the way through: by “the foreskin of the flesh” he means sin.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Israel’s assent to the law became a bond that Christ wiped out by His decrees.
comments.comment:
When the law that curses transgressors was given, all the people of Israel stood and shouted their assent to what was said and accepted it. Their assent became a kind of handwritten bond. Christ wiped out this bond, their assent to the law, by his own decrees. For he made rulings against the observances of the law. About foods, he ruled that it is not what goes into a man but what comes out of him that defiles him (Matthew 15:11). About keeping the Sabbath, he ruled by healing on the Sabbath. Anyone who looks will find many more of the same kind.

So first of all, by his decrees he abolished the punishments the law laid on sinners for their sin, and he granted forgiveness of sins and repentance that leads to salvation. And because the people said “Amen” to the curses (Deuteronomy 27:15–26), the bond was set down as if signed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the handwritten bond in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: By his cross Christ triumphed over the hostile powers, drove Satan from his tyranny, and pulled down death's power.
comments.comment: … For by his own cross Christ triumphed over the evil and hostile powers, nailing to the wood “the bond written against us” (Colossians 2:14–15). He drove Satan away from his tyranny over us, abolished the sin of the world, opened the gates of Hades to the spirits below, and pulled down the power of death.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what Christ's triumph on the cross accomplished.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ brought down the opposing powers by laying aside His flesh on the cross.
comments.comment: “Having stripped off the rulers and authorities, he made a public show of them, triumphing on the cross.” By stripping off and laying aside the flesh he brought down the opposing powers; so “having stripped off the rulers and authorities, he made a public show of them, triumphing over them in it.” Up to the cross and to death itself, it went unnoticed that our Lord was both God and Son of God. He astonished people with his miracles, but his body kept him veiled. That is why Satan tempted him: he wanted to find out whether he was the one the prophets had proclaimed, so that, if he learned that he was, he might block the saving plan. But the evil one got nowhere, because he could not find out; so for the time being Christ remained hidden.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the triumph over the powers in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: After fulfilling the saving plan Christ openly showed the Godhead with His body.
comments.comment: But once he had been nailed to the cross, had died, been buried and risen, and had fulfilled everything in the saving plan, he stripped off his hiddenness and showed openly, with his head uncovered, that the Godhead was there to be seen together with his body. The first work of God was the resurrection from the dead, then the ascent into heaven, and then the works done in his name through his servants and the other saints. So, having stripped off his hiddenness, he openly made a show of the opposing powers. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul called a festival kept on set days a 'part of a feast', hinting that a life lived by the divine Word is a complete and unceasing feast.
comments.comment: But the great number of those who are thought to believe, and who are not of such stature, are unwilling or unable to keep all days in this way, and so they need outward examples, perceived by the senses, to remind them, so that they do not drift away altogether (Hebrews 2:1). I think that Paul had this in mind when he called the festival kept on days set apart from the others a “part of a feast” (Colossians 2:16), and that by speaking in this way he hinted that the life lived at all times according to the divine Word is not “in part of a feast,” but in a feast that is complete and unceasing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the phrase 'part of a feast'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law is abolished, so Jews must not be obeyed about it, for it was a shadow.
comments.comment: “So let no one judge you.” He teaches that the law has been abolished, now that Christ has wiped out the bond that stood against us. He teaches too that the evil one has fallen, now that the Lord has stripped off the rulers and authorities and made an example of them. So he tells them not to obey any longer these things that Christ’s working has abolished. Do not, he says, be won over by Jews who try to persuade you to keep what is in the law. Those things were a shadow of the body of Christ, which is the church. A shadow runs ahead of the body, but it has no substance of its own. That is why he says: do not obey the law.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul forbids judgment about the law.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Once the body has come, the shadow is superfluous.
comments.comment: … Since, then, the ordinances of the law are the shadow, what is the body? What belongs to Christ is not shadow. So once the body has come, the shadow is superfluous.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Greeks must not draw believers into angel worship through their own reasoning.
comments.comment: And do not be won over by Greeks who draw you into worshipping angels or the elements of this world either; for they “intrude into things they have not seen”, seeking purification from their own mind and their own reasoning. So “let no one judge you” is said about the Jews, and “let no one rob you of the prize” about the Greeks. He means: let no one plot against you, now that you are already winning and getting the better of the evil one.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Calling angel worship humility abandons Christ, the head of every rule.
comments.comment: What sort of humility? The humility of saying: “We are lowly, and God is great, too great to be served by us. Since we cannot reach as far as him, we win his favour through his angels, and through them we are brought to him.” Earlier he said, “who is the head of every rule and authority” (Colossians 2:10), and now he says: why do you go to the elements and to angels, abandoning their head, which is Christ?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the false humility in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Every benefit reaches the whole body from the head, so believers must hold fast to Him.
comments.comment: Here he made plain the aim we have been speaking of: what moved him to write was that some people were urging others to approach God through angels. We must, he says, hold fast to the head, for God the Word is the head of the universe. Why, then, let go of the head and cling to the body? The power of the angels may serve as a joint that links two or more limbs, but the benefit still comes to all from the head: to angels as angels, to archangels as archangels, to visible things as visible things. Picture the heaven as the head of the world and the sun and moon as its eyes. Arrange each part of the world in this way, as limbs in their order, and you will find one body of the universe. As there is a soul in the body and the body belongs to the soul, so you will find the invisible powers in the visible things. But the head is more sovereign than all of these, and from it the benefit flows into the whole body, supplied, of course, from the head.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Rules forbidding touch and taste treat as forbidden what God gave to be used up.
comments.comment: … Why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to rules: “Do not taste, do not touch, do not handle”, things which all perish as they are used? He presents these as Greek doctrines, for in their error these people command that no one should touch or taste anything that has life. Yet all these things were given to human beings to be used up, that is, to be spent and consumed in the use and the needs of life. So “do not touch” what God has given is a rule “according to their commandments and their teachings”.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Harsh rules look like humility and self-control but spare living creatures against God’s purpose.
comments.comment: This means: be wary of these rules, I mean “do not handle, do not taste, do not touch”, which seem to make some sense, because abstaining from foods and refusing to pamper one’s own flesh with plenty is the mark of people who are humble-minded and do not spare the body. But although self-control is a fine thing, their second motive is impious. They abstain not only as people who have mastered the belly, but also as people who think they must not harm living creatures, which were given to be used up in the course of life. They want to be more merciful to the dumb animals than God is.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the false show of wisdom and humility in ascetic rules in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Our hidden life is eternal blessedness revealed at Christ’s coming.
comments.comment: “Our life is hidden” stands for the blessedness of eternal life, which will be revealed to all when the glory of Christ is also revealed at his second coming.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "our life is hidden" means in clear, accessible terms.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Those who keep the Savior's commandments have a share in his glory stored up with God, for their life is hidden with Christ until he is revealed.
comments.comment: … And how could those who keep the commandments of our Savior, and have trained themselves thoroughly in a life and conduct of shining distinction, not be filled with the highest joy? For them a share in his glory is stored up with God, wholly and surely. For it says: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory’ (Colossians 3:3–4). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Because sin is called flesh, sins are its members.
comments.comment: Just as he often calls sin “flesh”, so now, listing the members of the flesh, he names fornication, uncleanness and the rest; for these are the members of sin.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: We die to sin, not in the flesh, by making sin idle in us.
comments.comment: … We, however, do not die according to the flesh—how could we?—but to sin, as it is written (Romans 6:2); that is, we render sin idle and ineffective in ourselves by putting to death “the members that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed” (Colossians 3:5). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what putting the earthly members to death means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls sins members, as the Colossian passage shows by naming fornication, impurity and greed as the members to be put to death.
comments.comment: … To see that Scripture commonly calls sins “members”, read what this same apostle says to the Colossians: “Put to death your members that are on earth: fornication, impurity, and greed, which is the service of idols. Because of these things God's wrath comes upon the sons of unbelief. In these things you too once walked, when you lived in them” (Colossians 3:5–7). See how he calls “members” the things he identifies as sins. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows from the verse itself that Paul's "members" are sins.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Putting off a garment is a picture of putting off the old man and casting off sin with it, for the sake of Christ.
comments.comment: [The forty martyrs, told to strip:] … “We are not taking off a garment,” they said, “but we are putting away the old man, who is being corrupted according to the desires of deceit (Ephesians 4:22; Colossians 3:9). We thank you, Lord, that with this garment we cast off sin together with it. Since we put it on because of the serpent, let us take it off because of Christ. …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste

comments.capsule: The old man is the sinful mind; the new, the spiritual.
comments.comment: By “the old man” he means the mind set on sin, and by its members, evil deeds; by “the new man” he means the spiritual mind, and by its members, good deeds.
comments.selected_reason: Clearly defines what Paul means by the old man and the new man.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The image of the Creator is stamped on the soul that no longer has the old man with his deeds.
comments.comment: … He [Celsus] speaks, too, without even having stopped to consider in which part of man the “after the image” of God is stamped, and that it lies in the soul that either never had or no longer has “the old man with his deeds” (Colossians 3:9), a soul which, because it does not have these, is called “after the image” of the Creator (Colossians 3:10). …
comments.selected_reason: Says in what part of a person the image of God lies.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul is more precious than the body, for only the soul can receive the Creator's image.
comments.comment: … we say that the soul, and above all the rational soul, is a thing more precious than any body, since the soul can receive what is “according to the image of Him who created” it (Colossians 3:10), while the body cannot at all. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When believers think and do what belongs to Christ, he acts through them and is in them.
comments.comment: … This is like the words “that he may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). What he means is this: that God may work all things in all who set their minds on the things of God. When you think and do what belongs to Christ, he is the one acting through you, and he is in you.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Virtue is a divine garment, and putting on compassion means being adorned in a merciful and Christ-like way of life.
comments.comment: … for virtue is a divine garment. Thus also Paul exhorts: 'Put on the Lord Jesus' (Rom 13:14) and 'Put on the bowels of compassion' (Col 3:12), which is: be adorned in a merciful manner and in the Christ-like way of life; and again: 'Let us put on the armor of light' (Rom 13:12) to prepare ourselves to fight against the adversaries. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Love must lead the way, for without it no duty is completed.
comments.comment: Unless love leads the way, none of our duties is carried through to completion. It is when we love one another that we both keep from harming one another and take care to do one another good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why love is called the bond of perfectness in simple and practical terms.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Let the peace of Christ be your umpire, and thank Christ rather than seeking shelter in angels.
comments.comment: Do not let those who lead you astray, he says, rob you of the prize; let the peace of Christ be the umpire among you, so that you are united to Christ. “And be thankful.” To whom? To Christ, of course, who called you; and do not run to angels for shelter.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Masters must repay their slaves' goodwill with just and fair care.
comments.comment: Since your slaves, he [Paul] says, serve you with goodwill, you masters must also repay them justly and fairly, with the care that is fitting. So fairness answers to their goodwill.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul asks of masters in plain terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: If Christ were only a man there would be nothing deep to speak and no door to open, but since the Word became human we need God to open the door and grant us to speak the mystery.
comments.comment: “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving, praying also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of God for which I am also in bonds, that I may make it clear as I ought to speak.” (Colossians 4:2-4) If Christ is not God but only a human honored by divine grace, there is nothing deep in the mystery about him. What door would he need for making it plain and speaking as one ought? There is nothing great or hard in saying about a human that he is human by nature. But if the Word from God is proclaimed as having become human, then we need God himself — the one who opens the door and grants us to speak the mystery in the fitting way (Colossians 4:2–4).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The word of the saints is seasoned with grace and salt, and the salt hints at understanding.
comments.comment: … the salt hints at understanding. For the word of the saints is not senseless or foolish but, as it is written, seasoned with grace and salt (Colossians 4:6), and it gives grace to those who hear (Ephesians 4:29). Christ also said to them, ‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew 5:13). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what a speech seasoned with salt means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: We bring the word to each person in the way that suits his character and condition.
comments.comment: So we do not say to everyone who comes to us, “First believe that the one I am introducing to you is the Son of God.” Rather, we bring the word to each person in the way that suits his character and condition, for we have learned “to know how we ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:6). There are some to whom we preach this, since they can do no more than be urged to believe; to others we come, as far as we can, with proof by way of questions and answers.
comments.selected_reason: Shows what knowing how to answer each one looks like in practice.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
